review:
It's 2010. Me and the boys launch Halo Reach for the first time ever as we put Halo 3 back in it's case. We play invasion and then jump onto forge world. Forward to 2011 me and the boys are high ranks. Dominating any game we enter together. We then establish a large group of players to play custom games with. We played a lot of just Fat Kid lol. But then the game mode infection came out. And me and the boys suited up and played that game mode for 2 years straight. It's 2013. Most of the boys go silent. Few play Halo Reach. Some jump on to Halo 4, but it isn't the same. Slowly but surely me and including the boys go silent.

Fast forward to 2019 here i am. Playing the game that me and the boys thrived on. Though i have a new group of friends who are playing Reach. I can only hope that one day at least one of the boys will come back and play one more custom or infection game with me. Till then. It's time to relive to golden days and create new memories with it.

I remember when I was young I really wanted to play Halo 3 and Reach so much but I didn't have an Xbox 360... that was over a decade ago now and both these games have launched on PC here on MCC.

I cannot express how happy I am finally getting to play these games for the first time. The multiplayer made me feel like I was... young again... experiencing the games for the first time and living part of my childhood that I never had.

Thank you Microsoft for making my life-long dream come true.

WARNING! In order to download all of the games in the collection DO NOT use the in game menu to do so. It constantly fails and only downloads maybe one thing you selected. To download everything you want, just go into the properties in your steam library, click on DLC, and then select what you want. This is the only frustration free way of doing it!

No onto my REVIEW!
I absolutely love the Halo series. I suck at the game, all my friends are so much better, but that doesn't stop my love for the series. I remember the days of old, OG Xbox, sleeping over at my best friends house every weekend to beat Halo 1 CO-OP. Then Halo 2 came out, and we would beat Halo 1 then 2 CO-OP over night. Then Xbox 360 came out with Halo 3. So then we played Halo 1, 2 and 3 CO-OP. Sadly I have to move away before ODST came out, but by then the 360 was out of course, and we could play Xbox Live with voice chat. The new coming era of online gaming kept me and my best friend playing halo together for years to come, even with an entire country now between us. This is the beautiful story that so many of us share with Halo. Friendships and Needlers. 
The game works as it should, and now playing it on a pretty beefy PC in 1440p, it looks amazing! Just how your brain tries to think you remembered it, without any polygons. But of course you can press a button and bring it back and forth to see how it really looked, vs how your mind painted it in modern graphics for you.

Score 9.5/10
It was only a dream to imagine Halo coming back to PC and now it has come true. The Master Chief Collection definitely succeeds but is still a tiny bit rough around the edges in some aspects. No major issues in my experience such as crashes or start-up problems. My biggest gripe is that you cannot crouch while moving which feels very off. The framerate appears great, however, 100+ FPS here doesn't feel as quite as smooth as 100+ in other games. Haven't quite figured out as to why that is, or if it's just me, but my eyes adjusted anyway. I remember putting in many hours into Halo: Custom Edition (Combat Evolved) years ago so I've been looking forward to this.

In many ways, a great game, but with some problems. This review can basically be summed up with "All in-game = amazing, out-of-game = awful".
[h1] The Good [/h1]
[list]
[*] Gameplay is pretty much as good as it was 10 years ago, nice change from most shooters and is legendary.

[*] Graphics retain the original style while being nice and sharp. Nothing groundbreaking but it's nice to have a game that isn't post-processed to shit by tonnes of effects. 

[*] A lot of content, especially if you paid £7. Tonnes of gamemodes, maps, great campaign.

[*] Soundtrack so good I kept listening to it for 10 years and now there's finally a game to go with it again

[*] Strong playerbase and will be strong for a long time

[*] Some great options for a PC game, great fov changes and fps stuff etc

[*] Mod support I think, but hasn't taken off too much just yet.

[*] Great set of achievements, done properly for once with steam

[/list]
[h1] The Neutral [/h1]
[list]

[*]Nice control scheme, but rebinding is very limited.

[*] Runs well, but no real fine tuning you can do sadly

[*] Due to PC, balance is a bit skewed compared to console. Open maps are just DMRs rinsing you across the map whenever you peak. Can get a bit tiring but nothing major if that's the way the devs wanna go.

[/list]
[h1] The Bad [/h1]
[list]
[*] Originals had what everyone agrees was best halo customisation. Customisation went from 9/10 to 2/10, mainly from progression.

[*] Progression SUCKS, you level up every so often and unlock preset armour parts and stuff in a limited order. No more hype for buying a really cool piece of armour or armour effect and finally getting it. Everyone now looks the exact same and there is no choice over progression AT ALL. Along with that they removed all the cool ranks, now it has a generic system of level from tier 1 to tier 11 with boring sounding ranks and AWFUL icons (more on that later)

[*] Menu SUCKS compared to Reach's, which had possibly the best menu of all time. It is considerably harder to use, with a far worse style, not fitting Reach's vibes at all. It is all designed in the 343 Halo 4+ generic blue way, which isn't bad compared to most games but a crime to replace the original menu with.

[*] Service record, post game stats, icons, medals (more on that), all Halo 4+, and they are at most a 2/10 compared to the perfection of Reach's. Soulless super clean cartoony pictures compared to the gritty and much nicer colour pallette of the original. Ruins the tone of the game in the menus.

[*] Missing a lot of small features from the original. Forge, theatre are gonna be here for sure, but just so many tiny things that were great have been removed. [b]MAP VOTING PLEASE[/b]

[*] Kept the ruined-maps from infection, where 343 (?) made gutted versions of classic maps because they didn't like camping. Camping still exists, but maps are ruined with stupid colours and bits cut off. Could all be solved by including originals in pool and having voting but there is no logic to some of their changes.

[*] Minor technical issues: Sound is pretty ruined sometimes with crackling, and some people have input delay. Matchmaking can take ages sometimes etc

[*] Netcode is dodgy, so many trade kills which can really ruin games, like griffball with every single person having neutral KD

[*] Mentioned earlier, MAP VOTING is so needed and it is a crime to remove from reach, the game which really revolutionised map voting for gaming as a whole. There are great maps from the original which I haven't been able to play yet, while some bad maps have come up countless times. [b] MAP VOTING PLEASE [/b]

[/list]
[h1] Overall [/h1]
In game is great, could do with some fixes but is super fun. Progression, menu and customisation ALL [b]ruined[/b], couple of technical issues. These aren't just niche opinions, I have talked to 10s of people about this game, and not a single person likes the menu changes, icon, rank, progression changes etc.
However the gameplay, content and price are still worth it. Newcomers might be able to ignore the issues I mentioned. I love this game but it's so frustrating to see it come so close to perfection.
Overall: [b] 7/10 [/b]
Gameplay: [b] 9/10 [/b]
Graphics: [b] 7.5/10[/b]
Menu, outergame stuff, progression [b] 2/10 [/b]

Okay, I love the Halo series to death. It has given me so much joy and fun over the years... I've poured thousands upon thousands of hours in to the franchise as a whole and some individual titles, like Halo CE and 3, are among my favorite games ever. I played all of the titles in this collection at or near release on their original platforms.

All that to say: this collection needs work. As I write this review, I am nearing 500 hours on the steam version alone, not to mention the Xbox One version of MCC. There are several main issues with this version of MCC that will impact your enjoyment to varying degrees, depending on what modes you like more or what you find important in a PC port. Let me list them out, starting with a big one:

-Abysmal matchmaking system. This game has no ability to replace lost players on your team mid-game, and quitting is rampant. You can and will find yourself on the giving and receiving end of lopsided games, frequently. Teams are supposedly balanced (even in social gamemodes) to try and prevent this but in practice games where the majority of people playing are meaningfully contributing and having fun are very rare. AFK players, smurfs and assorted fun-sucking players are a big problem too. Ranked modes have low population, and therefore will match you with people way farther above or below your skill, but can in my experience lead to marginally more balanced and/or fun games than social, which is unexpected. You can still have fun in MM, but I would strongly recommend bringing friends along and not getting too invested in it as a competitive game.

-Technical issues are steadily being fixed but are still numerous and range from annoying to game breaking. Disconnects and crashes are a big source of frustration, especially in matchmaking and tragically are also a problem in coop campaign and Firefight modes. Xbox Live functionality is fickle, and windows generally has tons of obscure bugs and frustrations associated with it, but that's not exactly the game's fault. I will also warn that those who care about accurate and detailed game stats and achievements (which this games has tons of) are going to have a bad time. Halo MCC is notorious for glitched achievements, leaderboards and general statistics. Part of it is the game being buggy, and the other is the Halo Waypoint backend stuff that 343i uses to manage player stats is incredibly unreliable. I'm currently at 638/700 achievements and also care about stats, so it's a huge sore point for me.

-No in-game player blocking or reporting. Are you kidding?

-Hit registration, in some of the games in the collection, frankly sucks.

So this sounds really awful, right? Why is this game recommended? Well, to put it simply, a shoddy port of a great game is still worthwhile. I'm not a fan of Halo 4, but every other game in this collection, IMO, is goddamn amazing. Such a blast to play with friends, tight gunplay, creative level designs and fun weapon sandboxes and game mechanics abound. If you are new to Halo or have played the games before, I would totally recommend getting this collection and experiencing these formerly (for the most part) console-bound FPS masterpieces with a surprising amount of PC-centric upgrades that bring the games (when MCC isn't acting up) above and beyond.

The second reason I recommend this game, and perhaps even the most important one is that once 343i delivers a fully functional custom game browser (which they are in the process of doing) and official mod tools are released the game can realize it's true potential: a community-driven, highly customizable, moddable social FPS with tons of content, tight mechanics and a great way to make some friends on the internet

Halo MCC is not there yet, but it's close. It needs a push.
To all my fellow Halo fans old and new - here's hoping it gets it.

[h3][i]Permission to leave [b]Xbox, Phil.[/b] 
For what purpose [b]Master Chief[/b]?
To bring [b]Halo[/b] back to the [b]PC community[/b]!
...
Permission granted.[/i][/h3]

Finally, the highly praised [i]Halo[/i] franchise has released some of its best entries on PC, neatly assembled in one juicy collection. As someone who grew up only listening to how [i]Halo[/i] is great and Master Chief is a super-chad, after playing it, I can say, without a doubt, both statements are correct.

While the title does say [i]The Master Chief Collection[/i], we also get two spin-offs: [i]ODST[/i] and [i]Reach[/i], with the latter being my personal favourite in terms of story. Many seem to dislike it because of how bland Noble Team is. Personally, that never bothered me. They never were the focal point of the story. It was always the planet itself, Reach. Noble Team is nothing more than a surrogate pair of eyes for us to witness humanities struggle against overwhelming odds first-hand and the horrors enacted by the Covenant upon the inhabitants of Reach. As for [i]ODST[/i], it was ok. It takes place during [i]Halo 2[/i], but nothing from its story was particularly memorable. Some quirky moments and funny dialogue, but nothing more than that.

Still, the title clearly says - [i]The Master Chief Collection[/i], so let's get back to his escapades. I may get some flak for this, but [i]Halo: Combat Evolved[/i] has the worst story, if you can even call it that. There was barely anything. It felt more like a concept. Don't get me wrong, [i]Halo 4[/i] is right next to it, but I still consider [i]Halo: Combat Evolved[/i] worse. But then...BAM! [i]Halo 2[/i]. We get more lore about this universe, more epic cutscenes, more chad one-liners, and characters actually have some personality. And it is here that Master Chief actually became a chad, with subsequent entries continuing to expand the legend that is [i]Sierra-117[/i]. So, even with a few blemishes, [b]I immensely enjoyed this sci-fi space epic[/b]; From witnessing the glassing of Reach, helping a friend go out with a bang, to detonating a nuke above Earth like a true chad, there was never a lack of memorable moments.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2676858881

But what about the gameplay?

Well, it's simply fantastic, and this much is true for every [i]Halo[/i] game. Each entry improves upon its predecessor, refining the gameplay, but at the same time, staying true to that familiar gameplay loop set in stone by [i]Halo: Combat Evolved[/i]. Personally, I have [i]Halo 3[/i] as my top pick. It's the culmination of Bungie's trilogy, and its greatness and epicness during gameplay are still unrivalled by any previous or subsequent [i]Halo[/i] games.

But, where are my manners; I have yet to speak about the gunplay itself. So let's fix that, shall we - [b][i]it's an FPS game where you shoot, throw grenades and drive vehicles.[/i][/b] But the driving controls are unusual. Rather than driving, I dunno, like in 99.9% of games, with movement keys, [i]Bungie[/i] said: "We don't do that here", and instead, your mouse is the steering wheel. Tricky at first, but once you get the hang of it, you'll be drifting on the surface of halo rings like the great Colin McRae.

Each new entry does try to up the ante, spicing up the gameplay, just ever so slightly. [i]Halo 2[/i] has Chief [b]dual wield[/b] smaller weapons, which he seemingly forgot how to do in [i]Halo 4[/i] after his cryo-sleep. With [i]Halo 3[/i] came [b]one-time use equipment[/b]; Useless overall, but they do look neat in the promotional CGI trailer. However, soon after, an unfathomable evil shook the very heavens, as long and fierce wars were waged over its place in the Halo-verse, with many brave souls lost in the process. Just speaking its name aloud invokes thousand years of bad luck upon your no scope 360 trick shots. I am, of course, talking about [b]sprinting.[/b] This putrid thing first reared its ugly head in [i]Halo: Reach[/i], but only as an [b]armour ability[/b]. It wasn't until [i]Halo 4[/i] that [b]it[/b] finally infected Master Chief, becoming his innate ability. Truly a sad day for [i]Halo[/i] fans all over the galaxy. But then again, he was often seen sprinting in cutscenes...

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2643717100

Sprinting polemics aside, I love how [i]Halo[/i] effortlessly creates a heterogeneous battlefield. Encounters pit you against a group comprised of unique enemy units, each with different strengths, weaknesses and mannerisms. We have [b][i]bird boys, smol boys, wort boys, bug boys, hairy boys, chunky boys, etc.[/i][/b] And while headshots mean instant death, some enemy units must be first stripped bare; hairy boys have armour, wort boys have shields, etc. Do note - each protection is weaker against different ammo. For example, wort boy shields are strong against human bullets but weak to plasma-based weapons. But, I will let you in on a little secret - [b][i]All enemies and shields are weak to rockets to the face.[/i][/b]

While massacring half of the known universe is fun, sometimes we need to stop, take a breath and admire the scenery. And this is where [i]Halo [b]got me[/b]. Halo[/i] isn't like that hot chick who doesn't know she's hot. [i]Halo[/i] knows and wants your gaze. So, while [i]Halo: Combat Evolved[/i] has inner beauty and [i]Halo 4[/i] is entirely flat, the others were a succulent journey for the senses; From the Covenant and its many species, the mysterious biomes of the halo rings and the burning cities of Reach, all the way to Johnson and his clean-shaven chin that accentuates his magnificent moustache, the [i]Halo[/i] universe is beaming with beauty to behold.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2676656284

Yet, visual beauty can't work solo. Its age-old accomplice - music, plays a vital role in immersing the player within the games universe. Sadly, this is where a crucial issue occurred, as how does one rate [b][i]perfection[/i][/b]? 
Also, Keith David...Mmmm, you can be my Arbiter any day ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°). 

But, besides Keith David making my knees weak with his stern, thick and firm voice, sound effects in [i]Halo[/i] play a crucial role in perceiving one's surroundings. Being informed about various things during the chaotic fights is paramount for success - possible grenade explosion, what weapons the enemy is firing, etc. All produce distinct sound effects, which in turn help you avoid and instead inflict death upon the enemy.

But before we say farewell, I want to make something clear - I didn't partake in multiplay shenanigans, as I don't care for it. Thus, I can't provide insight into that part of the collection. But if that is what interests you, I highly suggest you read [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/Zionyx/recommended/976730/]the review from Zionyx[/url].

And with that said, I think it's pretty clear how I feel about [i]Halo[/i]. Thus, I'll finish by answering three quintessential questions any buyer may ponder about:

Where is [i]Halo? -[b]On Steam[/b][/i]. 
Who is [i]Halo? -[b]The big green dude[/b][/i]. 
Why is [i]Halo? -[b]Yes[/b][/i].

For context, I have most, if not all, the single-player achievements and have beaten all of the games included in Halo MCC. I played this collection after many patches and only had a few issues with crashes and freezing in Halo 4.

The games are some of the best in gaming history, with each offering something of value. They can frequently be picked up for dirt cheap during sales, so they are worth a buy even if, like me, you only play single-player primarily. Whether you are defending Reach, helping Master Chief survive against impossible odds, going feet first into hell or putting the Gravemind in its place underfoot, The Halo MCC Collection has something to offer anybody who likes games in the FPS genre. 

That said, like many studios these days, it is unfortunate that the community management team continues to needlessly politicize every event they can against community wishes. It warms my heart that the community manager who banned me for stating that as a gamer with a disability, I do not appreciate being tokenized with a nameplate is no longer employed. I asked to be unbanned, and my request was refused.

It is not nearly as bad as Infinite, but that game shows how even the greatest of franchises can fall flat if made for the modern audience. The other thing is the requirement for a 3rd party login, which should not be necessary when playing on Steam. 

Overall, Halo MCC has some great games, but it has terrible community management that likes to virtue signal and censor people and an unnecessary 3rd party login. Buy it if you want to experience gaming history before all these modern woke games, but be warned that putting the wrong opinion in forums or on announcements can get you banned. You also need a Microsoft account.
It's 2007, Soulja Boy crank that music video was posted on Youtube, You open Myspace to post about your epic day, Spider-Man 3 just hit movie theaters, And a game Called Halo 3 Just came out...

Although The Master Chief Collection was in an egregiously embarrassing state for several years, it's now probably the greatest deal in gaming now. Every FPS Halo game from CE to 4, with campaign, multiplayer, forge, firefight, theater, and more now readily available and accessible (plus mod support). For this review, I will be breaking it down by each individual game within the collection in release order:

Halo: Combat Evolved - Groundbreaking for its time, Halo CE has not aged perfectly, but it is still a blast to play over 20 years later. The level design can get pretty repetitive, with many assets being reused in multiple missions, CE still offers a very satisfying FPS experience, featuring a lot of open areas that allows you to tackle missions in drastically different ways. The different enemy types provide a hard enough challenge and the world of Installation 04 is unraveled in an engaging way. The sandbox is fairly simple looking back, but like other FPS games at the time, each weapon fulfilled a specific role, but the CE Magnum (or, the "Halo 1 Pistol") is of course extremely overpowered. In MCC, both the original 2001 release of the game and the 2011 Anniversary version are both playable and can be switched at will, even while playing a mission. The score might actually be the single best part of this game and each piece perfectly compliments the section it was made for. In MCC, CE has received probably the most new content as multiplayer customization was extremely limited in the original and Anniversary releases.

Halo 2 - Although CE established Halo as a monumental title, Halo 2 is where Halo truly came into form. Despite a rushed release in 2004, leading to cut content and several bugs, Halo 2 is a ton of fun. In the inverse of CE, Halo 2's level design is mostly made up of tighter spaces and a more focused experience, and doesn't have as many reused assets and environments. However, the story is much more polished and nuanced, featuring the playable perspective of the Arbiter in addition to the Master Chief. Halo 2 also introduces dual-wielding to the sandbox along with several new weapons and enemies like the infamous Brutes. Originally, H2 also served as the flagship for Xbox Live online multiplayer, so the multiplayer here feels much more attended to than CE. For hardcore players, the only significant issue regarding Halo 2 is the Legendary difficulty and LASO (Legendary All Skulls On) experience. Because of the rushed release, these difficulties were bugged and made extremely more difficult and unforgiving than any other in the franchise. MCC also served as the launch of the Anniversary edition of Halo 2, featuring a graphical overhaul for the campaign and new pre-rendered CG cutscenes, as well as a whole new multiplayer built on the Halo 4 engine.

Halo 3 - Not only my favorite game in the series, but my favorite game of all time. Halo 3 originally served as the conclusion to Master Chief's story and Bungie's original Halo trilogy in 2007. The story's complexity definitely takes a step back here, but does feel the most grand and epic, which does fit as the conclusion piece of the story. Halo 3 also arguably features the best level design in the series, with most missions boasting more unique environments and experiences, and returning to the more open style akin to CE. The multiplayer is definitely approved on from Halo 2 and additionally features some of the most iconic maps in the franchise. Halo 3 also introduces Forge, a creative mode where the player can create their own maps using structural and game-modifying tools. On top of this, Halo 3 added a Theater mode, so you can save clips and screenshots from previous campaign playthroughs or multiplayer matches. Halo 3 only received a slight graphical update for modern systems but has been upgraded with new customization content, as well as maps and assets from the cut Halo Online game.

Halo 3: ODST - Not originally part of MCC (as Master Chief does not technically appear in the game), Halo 3: ODST is probably the most underrated game in the franchise. Initially planned as a DLC for Halo 3, ODST became its own "full" game released in 2009. The campaign is relatively short and (in the original release) only included Halo 3's multiplayer system. Despite the campaign's short length, it features a unique neo-noir atmosphere and story, with an even more unique jazz score you don't get anywhere else in the series. Additionally, ODST introduces the popular Firefight mode, a wave-based survival mode with several maps and modifiers.

Halo: Reach - Like ODST, Reach was not originally part of MCC (even though he does appear as an Easter Egg in one cutscene). Serving as Bungie's swan song for the Halo franchise in 2010, this would be Bungie's last Halo game before leaving Microsoft and Halo to work on the Destiny IP instead. Halo Reach acts as a prequel to Halo CE, establishing the context for Master Chief's escape that results in finding the Halo ring. The story is more emotionally-driven, following the Spartans who defended Reach until the last moment. The multiplayer is deemed as fairly controversial as it took a more modern approach to FPS gaming, including elements like weapon classes, armor abilities, and bloom. However, the multiplayer contains a pretty fun experience and arguably has the best armor customization in the series. Firefight returns here as well.

Halo 4 - The only game made by 343 Industries in the collection, Halo 4 serves as the new beginning for Halo after Bungie's departure. Halo 4's campaign goes for a different approach, taking a more character-driven style, focusing on the relationship between Master Chief and his AI Companion, Cortana. The game also brings in a new art style that is quite jarring but ends up being fine. Halo 4 also adds a new faction of enemies and several new weapons to the sandbox. The worst part of Halo 4 is the new mode included in the game: Spartan Ops. As its replacement for Firefight, Spartan Ops are little missions that act as a kind of epilogue/spin-off of the main story. The levels are re-used campaign environments and are incredibly repetitive. That being said, Spartan Ops is a totally optional experience in understanding the overall story.

Halo: The Master Chief Collection - The collection as a whole provides some cross-game campaign playlists and in multiplayer you can queue up for any combination of the games in it. For multiplayer progression, a battle pass system is featured that last forever and adds a lot of content to the game.

To reiterate, the Master Chief Collection is a highly recommended game, being fun for both casual players and completionists (has 700 achievements!!).

This isn’t a critique of the games themselves — they’re good — it’s about the onerous Microsoft sign-in required to play after buying the game.

You can’t just launch and play. A Microsoft account is mandatory, account creation/verification is cumbersome and unreliable, and the sign-in servers are often flaky. Even single-player or offline modes demand a linked Microsoft account; owning the game on Steam isn’t accepted as proof. The mandatory Xbox/Microsoft sign-in is unnecessary (no cross-play) and harms the experience.

If you don’t mind dealing with that unstable, intrusive sign-in, go ahead; otherwise I can’t recommend buying it.

Halo's arrival on PC was a great occasion to experience such an important series for the history of console shooters. Halo stood out with it’s unique sci-fi setting, allowing weapons, enemies and environments to expand upon the gameplay of the conventional shooter. All of this is brought to life by an effective aesthetic, the colourful and gritty art style sets a great tone, but a special commendation goes to Martin O' Donell's epic soundtracks that litter the series. These elements are what made Halo initially stand out, and have become a point of inspiration in their high quality execution.

[h1]Halo: Combat Evolved[/h1]
What an explosive intro to the series. Immediately, Combat Evolved maintains a steady climactic pace as many of the series’ staple mechanics and tropes are introduced. The new visuals are kind of cluttered, but the older graphics still pop out with a beautiful visual flair thanks to the bright colours. It’s the first iteration, so the mechanics feel a bit dated and rough, especially with enemy AI, but it’s saved by beautiful level design. That first level thrusts you deep into tight corridors packed with aggressive aliens, contrasted beautifully by the giant fields that follow, giving you a vast amount of freedom. Every level tackles a new memorable style that became essential to later Halo experiences, from the giant battlefields of Silent Cartographer, to the brief trips into horror in Guilty Spark. Unfortunately, the game takes a sharp dive in quality from “The Library” til the end, reusing a lot of areas and just generally being a lot less fun to navigate. Combat Evolved is a brilliant opening to the franchise, but does unfortunately suffer from it’s age and unsatisfactory final third.

[h1]Halo 2[/h1]
Halo 2 is deeply appreciable as an expansion to Combat Evolved, insistent on building on the original as much as possible for better or for worse. Halo 2 has received an extremely faithful visual recreation, enhancing the raw graphical power while keeping the beautiful colours and lights, The CG Cutscenes especially show how much care was put into this remake. In terms of gameplay, a lot of new elements have been added such as hijacking and dual wielding, small changes that shake up the formula and are complemented by new weapons and vehicles. 2 introduction of the Arbiter places the world through a new perspective, bringing an larger world to appreciate, but this is also where Halo 2’s main problem lies. With 2 intertwined campaigns, Halo 2 feels bloated, a lot of levels stretch further than they should and the story feels a bit rough in the middle sections. Regardless, 2 still brings enough new content to be a worthy sequel to experience.

[h1]Halo 3[/h1]
The original conclusive entry, Halo 3 continues to further expand the ideas within the series, but feels less meaty than the other entries. I think this game went the hardest with its brightly coloured armours and aliens, and I think it really paid off as the blend of realistic grit and simple stand out colours blends really well in the artstyle. Returning to Combat Evolved, Halo 3 feels brilliantly executed, with tight pacing and almost every level having interesting and memorable design. The content that’s there is great, it stands as the culmination of the series’ strengths so far, but it does feel a tad lacking, due to a notable decrease in levels, some of which are extremely short. It’s further emphasised by the difficulty, Halo 3 is weirdly easier than the rest of the series due to a number of factors, resulting in a lacking difficulty curve and some epic moments that can feel a bit too easy. Halo 3 is great, but it does leave me feeling like the game could've used a bit more content.

[h1] Halo 3: ODST [/h1]
ODST's a weird experiment that doesn't quite pay off, but still gets some things right. With a more open structure, ODST excels in it's portrayal of New Mombasa. The quiet city streets beautifully emphasise that feeling of loneliness, the dark environments void of friendly company leave you avoiding enemies, all accompanied by a haunting jazz melody that gives the city a Noir flair. Halo's usually best in co op, but this game was really made to be experienced alone, the ideas it's pioneering here predate a lot indie games that would carry this atmosphere further. It's a shame then ,that the actual city really fails to live up to it's atmosphere. Traversing Mombasa quickly reveals repeated environments, lacking in creativity and feeling bland, a sense that applies to most of the combat levels interspersed throughout. I don't think the game did enough with the ODST idea either, you're not meant to be a super soldier, but the only real change is cut weapons and health packs returning from Combat Evolved. I think they should've leaned into the stealthy elements way further, but you still feel like a killing machine in every mission, which isn't helped by the atrocious archetypes that most of the main characters fill, very boring characters. ODST tried something new, it's not a perfect result but I still admire it for the few amazing moments it got right.

[h1] Halo: Reach [/h1]
Bungie's swan song combines all the lessons learned over the franchise into a beautiful package that sends off the developer. Reach once again plays with quiet moments and focusing on an entire team like ODST, but pulling the ideas into a condensed linear narrative was a great call. Noble Team's lineup of diverse intimidating soldiers can feel underwritten at times, but their prominence in narrative and gameplay gives Reach a unique feeling of camaraderie. Reach also takes the climatic scope of 2 and 3, all the levels fill you with awe and intensity, but it's pacing feels more like Combat Evolved, with a steady stream of missions that all feel independent and pay homage to various points in the series. Despite how much this game owes to its predecessors, It's amazing how Reach still feels so different.  Playing a smaller role in the war feels much different in a way I think ODST wanted to capture, and the introduction of Armour Abilities lead to one of favourite shakeups to Halo's combat. My only complaint is the artstyle, colours feel way more washed out now, which is tonally fitting, but it makes me miss the brighter look of the previous games. Reach is the culmination of a franchise and Bungie did a fantastic job implementing every lesson they learned into an amazing game.

[h1] Halo 4 [/h1]
The move to the new developer is quite apparent, as Halo 4 doesn’t quite hold the same charm it’s predecessors had. There are a few new welcome ideas, mainly the Promethean enemies that add a new layer to some encounters, but many of the weaponry added fails to be interesting and fulfil the same roles existing weapons already had. They’ve also altered. the look and sound of almost everything in the game, leading to most enemies and weapons looking far more generic and missing their uniqueness, especially in the boring sounds of most alien weapons. There’s a bigger narrative emphasis too, which would be fine if the writing wasn’t so mediocre, it’s nice the characters speak a bit more now but everything falls flat, mainly the very bland villain. Halo is no longer the juggernaut in gaming it once was in the 00’s, and playing this entry very quickly reveals why; it’s merely decent as best, and far below the standards of the series.

To be honest, I didn’t have Xbox or played Halo before. So, a bundle/collection which I could grab easily & cheaply for PC like this was really beneficial for me as a newcomer. Here’s my short impression of each games.

Halo: CE
The first game and our introduction to Master Chief, Cortana, and the premise of the series. I can’t help but to compare the feel and gameplay of Halo CE to Half-Life, another scifi FPS released around that time. It has fun gun combat and enemies AI are quite smart. The story is intriguing, but rather slim. The campaign is quite lengthy and has few varieties in terms of approach to gameplay. The only downside for me is that it relies heavily in long & mostly empty tunnels/ corridors/ vehichle section to “hide” or load the next area/section of the game beforehand.

Halo 2
It improves almost everything from the first game, with stuffs like alternate story campaign/levels as the arbiter to dual wielding guns. The story & setting are also really interesting. I also have to give a shoutout to game options of altering between original & anniv graphic mode in Halo CE & 2 almost instantly. The downside is, of course, the abrupt & infamous cliffhanger ending.

Halo 3
A conclusion to Master Chief’s trilogy. It ties major plot points throughout the series quite nicely, while also going out with a bang. The gameplay stays the same with some tweaks here & there. Devs in Bungie tried to spice things up a bit & it was mostly a success, at least for me.

Halo 3: ODST
A drastic departure from the first trilogy, as you are not playing as Master Chief, but a normal everyday soldier on a doomed battlefield. It is quite darker & has a detective noir feel to it. The story campaign is sort of a spinoff of the main series with jazz-style musics accompanying you throughout the game. It also has unusual approach to level-based gameplay, with accessible hub world & (mostly) non-linear storytelling.

Halo: Reach
A sort of prequel to Halo series & the last game made by Bungie. The game mixes everything from previous games while also improves on it. Reach tells an engaging story with likeable cast of characters in Noble team’s struggles during the fall of reach. For me, the game has the right amount of fun and doesn’t overstay its welcome. The highlights are the flying section in outer orbit & the gut-wrenching ending.

Halo 4
The first game by 343 Industries for the new era of Halo. It continues the story of Master Chief & Cortana with a twist. Among the other games in the collection, it is the shiniest & the newest one of the bunch. The gameplay formula stays mostly the same; with new weapons, new environments, new allies and new enemies. The story campaign on this one is short compared to the rest.

Overall, I had enjoyable time with Halo MCC. It is a great collection with good value & bang for the buck on PC.

It's Halo. An iconic game series that has it's influence across all modern shooters today. For the price of the entire collection you get 6 Halo games. Halo CE, Halo 2 and Halo 3 are considered masterpieces in the gaming world, a must play. Halo Reach and Halo 3 ODST are very good games in their own right. While Halo 4 has flaws, the game is still pretty decent. All in all, none of the games in the collection are really "bad" per se.

The singleplayer campaigns are very worth it, that experience has been relatively untainted by the porting to PC. In many ways, it has even improved the graphical quality of the original games significantly. The full campaign experience of all the Halo games here are very worth it and is something you should definitely be interested in playing. Do a blind playthrough of all the games. I personally recommend playing the games in the release order.

However, there are definitely some flaws in the multiplayer right now. At least when it comes to online matchmaking. Controller players are given aim assist so incredibly powerful that it makes using keyboard+mouse a direct disadvantage. A lot of matches with ranged weapons in general and very dumbed down and dull on the pc version. Ranged weapons in close-quarters maps isn't an issue since those matches rely entirely on who can best use the weapons to get kills. However in large maps, such as those in vehicles, ranged weapons are far more powerful than you would think. It's bad enough that people pretty much avoid using vehicles so they don't get spammed from across the map and die before they can use them. It's not fun to play a match where sitting back in spawn with a ranged weapon and shooting across the map is more effective than using vehicles or power weapons.

Another major issue is with the servers themselves. Because of a low playerbase, EU players suffer immensely. I imagine the same will be true for all regions except NA. You're usually forced onto US servers where you're at a disadvantage. There are many other bugs with the multiplayer such as Halo 3's hitreg being godawful but right now the online multiplayer has some serious bugs that need to be fixed. 343 is continuing to work on the game and hopefully they eventually fix some of the bugs that are present. Halo's multiplayer is good but there are some major flaws that prevent it from reaching it's former glory.

That being said, hosting custom game lobbies with custom modes and maps still provides limitless fun and entertainment for you and your friends. It's a good way to balance out the current problems with online matchmaking right now. Halo's custom games have the potential to be some of the most fun experiences you can have in gaming so I recommend you try them out at some point.

Other features exist like Firefight which is a PvE mode where you have to survive against hordes of enemies. There's also Forge which lets you build your own custom maps that you can share and play in custom games. There is also theater mode which lets you take screenshots and record clips of gameplay. All these features play a part in what makes Halo so great.

As of this review however, only Halo Reach, Halo CEA and Halo 2 have released on PC. The rest have not released yet but are in the works. Buying the entire bundle buys all 6 games, it's just that not all of them have released yet. When they release, you will get them. Some of the features I mentioned in the review such as Forge and Theater have not fully released yet either but are coming.

My final verdict is that the entire bundle is worth it. If there is a sale however, it's a must-buy. When all the games finally release it may very likely become a must-buy. It absolutely will become a must-buy if they manage to fix all the bugs.

There are plans to add input-based matchmaking in the future, which could separate k&m players from controller players so that the powerful aim assist can be avoided if you wish to.

The Halo franchise from Combat Evolved - Reach is bar none my favorite series of games. Words cannot describe how ingrained each game is to my childhood, the titanic waves of emotions I’ve felt, and the dear memories/friends I made along the way! All of which compels me to yap way too long about this remastered collection. Next paragraph is my TL;DR thoughts.

Despite one of the worst video game launches of all time and some persisting issues, The Master Chief Collection in its current state is solid. It’s very much worth the full asking price, nevermind the sale price. It’s just sadly apparent once Microsoft's plan to monetize cosmetics failed, they cut support prematurely. This resulted in some problems and half-baked features that were never finished. For example, did you know that only 2 of the 6 campaigns support cross-play? There’s also some collection-wide graphical and mechanical issues that make the games all look and play a little bit worse than normal. Finally, none of the original menus, loading screens, and credit sequences are included. These all really creatively contributed to the tone of each game, so it's a shame they've all been cut.
That all being said, I’d be lying to everyone if I said that MCC’s enhancements didn’t make up for these shortcomings. If you'd like to see summaries of my individual campaign thoughts, a "2026 rating", and my recommended order to play through the story, keep reading.

1. Halo: Combat Evolved - 8/10
Halo: CE's campaign is best experienced using the Halo: REBALANCED mod with classic audio. You lose out on the remastered visuals, but those aren't very well polished and are generally hated on by the community for not being faithful to CE's unique design.

Halo CE not only completely redefined what a “console shooter” could be, but 25 years later its impact can STILL be felt in almost every shooter that comes out. I still remember "playing" The Silent Cartographer demo disk at my neighborhood friend's house back when we were 6 or 7. His parents noticed how absolutely in love we were with it, and later purchased him the full game and Halo 2. We were hooked.

The overall art direction and gameplay are some of the best in the entire gaming medium. Given its emphasis on those things, it’s also very easy to overlook just how much happens in its underrated story. Sure it’s mostly world building and surface level campy action, but it still feels inspired, holds up, and beautifully sets up the more involved stories the sequels tell. Unfortunately, it's also clear that this was made by a small team even by 2001 standards. Simple and dated design goals like remixed assets and backtracking levels take center stage in the third act, and are probably the parts of the games that have aged the worst. Thankfully, Halo: REBALANCED does a lot to tastefully alleviate issues like this.

2. Halo 2 - 9/10
If you'd like to use the fantastic remastered audio/visuals, then go ahead and play vanilla. If you want a better overall experience using the original audio/visuals, play the Halo 2: REBALANCED mod. It's the definitive way to experience Halo 2.

What Halo: CE's campaign did for console shooters mechanically, Halo 2 did for narrative and budget. The only noteworthy con for Halo 2 vanilla is that the moment-to-moment gameplay is probably the weakest in the series. But for the shooter genre as a whole, it’s still a high bar that's really fun to experience. Also go ahead and pretend the Legendary difficulty doesn't exist, unless you REALLY like pain. There's a couple small quirks with the MCC version of this game too, but it's nothing worth getting into. It's easily the game that received the most love.

3. Halo 3: ODST - 10/10
This is my favorite game in the series, and the only time I'd recommend someone to play these games out of release order. Halo: CE sets the stage, Halo 2 fleshes out one side of the conflict, and ODST handles another before the epic conclusion. That being said, if you're planning to play this one for the first time, there's two things that you should be aware of.

First, you owe it to yourself to find and listen to the 30 logs throughout the city as you play through the story. This isn't a small side-story like most story collectibles in games, this IS the A-story of the game, which interweaves with the third act of what you're playing through beautifully. This "detective clue-finding" style of gameplay is prevalent throughout the main story, and the city exploration sections are intentionally designed so you have enough time to listen to these while you make your way to the next objective. The game feels incomplete without doing this.

Second, while co-op is always a great time, ODST is the one I recommend people play solo for your first time. Only caveat I would make here is if your friend(s) are very quiet.

But yeah, I adore so much about this game. The only thing I could ever complain about it is that it's getting old, and long overdue for a sequel or remake of some kind. Microsoft also mismanaged the original release of this Halo 3 expansion, instead deciding to release it as a fully priced standalone game. But thankfully that’s not an issue anymore.

4. Halo 3 - 8.5/10
The late night of September 24 2007 outside my local GameStop with my dad and neighborhood best friend is a memory I'll never forget. Halo 2 split-screen tournaments, game fuel, a MASSIVE line throughout the mall. We were pretty close to the front of the line, and were the first ones to buy a copy of that beautiful Legendary edition. It was a hell of a night.

This jump started a tradition of going to midnight launches with friends for years until the rise of digital ownership killed it off. For anyone who may not be aware, the hype behind this game was unprecedented at the time. This was prime-time in the golden age of AAA video games, where budgets started to bloom but creatives were still able to achieve their uncompromising vision. And the best part? Halo 3 lived up to that hype, and we finished the fight.

EPIC is the word I would use to describe Halo 3's campaign. Everything feels properly important and dramatic, even if the writing is a step down from the earlier three games. Despite that, the second half is unbelievably satisfying, and the gameplay feels like a proper return to form after Halo 2. It manages to find a perfect balance between CE and 2's design and is considered to have the best “gameplay feel” out of the entire franchise by a huge portion of the player base, myself included.

Side but important point, I have no idea if this is an MCC exclusive issue or if this was present in the original release, but none of the Arbiter's voice lines will play in-game if a player is controlling him in co-op. This really undercuts a lot of the narrative momentum with him after Halo 2 and should definitely be fixed.

5. Halo: Reach - 9/10
An encore send-off by Bungie before they moved on to Destiny. This is the “better Rogue One” of the franchise and cements just how well this team understands the video game medium. From the beginning, you know how it ends.

I recently replayed through this campaign and was stunned at how modern the design of this game still feels, despite being almost 15 years old now. While it’s up for debate, this game also has the best audio/visual art in the series. I can’t even mention Reach without hearing those haunting chants that permeate throughout the entire soundtrack. While the gameplay shoots for new heights, the story also manages to take all of the lessons learned from each game, and mix it into a big fan favorite. This is a fantastic prequel best experienced after you’ve played through the previous 4 stories, albeit with some problems in structure due to some cuts late in development.

I’d yap more about this one, but unfortunately I’m hitting the character limit.

Halo 4 - 6/10

The moment has finally arrived for the entire Master Chief Collection to arrive on PC since the first release of Halo on the original Xbox in 2001 all the way to the remastered version in 2011, and continued on to end of 2012 with the release of Halo 4! Here is what I have now so far.

[h1][b][u]Characters[/u][/b][/h1]
Halo: Reach—You play as Noble Six, part of the NOBLE team—Carter, Catherine, Jun, Emile, and Jorge—who are called upon to push back the Covenant forces that are invading the planet Reach. Each character has their own strengths and weaknesses, and personalities that make them unique.
Halo: CE—
--Master Chief: you maul down cowering Grunts, courageous Elite forces, and flood forms with your weaponry at your disposal. Each non-player character have their own likable personalities and it makes them more complex, especially the relationship between Cortana and MC.
--The Monitor acts like a big-know-it-all, egotistical sphere that talks, but Sentinels are there to help defend and distract you from his blabbering.
--Johnson is great in this one, and happened to be cloned.
Halo 2—
--Master Chief: a pleasure as always and looks awesome
--The Arbiter may not be the same experience as the Chief, but you get to experience the perspective of the most prominent, willful figures of the Covenant that have sacrificed their lives to keep the Covenant force together.
--Johnson: his lines and personality are great, if not better in this one.
--Cortana: On par with the first game and plays a bigger role. Plus her model in both old and new graphics are more ideal
--Gravemind: Flood poet/scholar
Halo 3—You just play as Master Chief. Perhaps the fans didn't think The Arbiter was that fun to play as, so he's more of an ally in this installment, but in the end it's cool to see his transformation.
--Johnson is in this one and helps you in the end.
--The relationship between Cortana and Chief start to reach new heights.
--Of course, the powerful Gravemind is more intimidating.

Halo 3: ODST—This time it's much different than any Halo game; you play as an orbital drop shock trooper and observe the post-destruction of the slip-space rupture caused by a Covenant ship, and at the same time you are more of a detective who discovers artifacts left behind by fellow teammates and live through them, and liberating a Covenant species before manipulating it.

Halo 4—You play as the Chief again, and this time his personality becomes more dynamic than any of the three previous games combined. More human, if you will.

[h1][b][u]Atmosphere[/u][/b][/h1]
All the games in general have gorgeous, open-word environments and closed-off, tight corridor environments, and each one fits the levels perfectly. Spaceships, the Halo ring, The Library, dense forests, snowy fields, beaches, and more. Halo: CE recycles a couple of maps but does it very well. All the other ones have their unique level designs.

[h1][b][u]Gameplay[/u][/b][/h1]
Controls for each game are smooth as butter, even on 60fps and/or unlimited frames. Controls can be bound to any key and there is instant controller swapping on the fly. Skulls can be turned on to change the gameplay dramatically for any game. Overall, it's really fun, but there are a few notes:
Halo: Reach—flying controls make take some time getting used to because you control and lock the height and you may easily get lost.
Halo 2—The difficulty Legendary is very unbalanced; your shield is pertinent for survival, and if you are exposed to any plasma fire you are dead within seconds.
Halo 3—I recommended that you do NOT turn the non-scoring skulls and play it on Legendary because it makes the first Scarab battle (The ARK) very difficult to the point of aggravation and frustration. I only got past it by using a tank and manipulating the scripting sequence so it would stay near the sea, and at one point it was pushed to the boundary and it retreated out of bounds
Halo 3:ODST—Plays very well, although can be very tough in matchmaking modes.
Halo 4—Co-op is bound to the main character when it comes to action sequences and it's not very well communicated. Plus, the ammo that you receive from Sentinel Knights is very little to none, and the wooded snipers early in this game are deadly.

[h1][b][u]Enemies/Allies[/u][/b][/h1]
—Enemies in each game have their own strengths and weaknesses:
-Grunts are weak and are usually in the front
-Elites are stronger with shields and enemies cower when they are killed
-Jackals have shields (except snipers) that protect them but they are more vulnerable to grenades and weapons that destroy their shields
-Hunters are very vulnerable in Halo 1 and require more precision to kill in Halo Reach, Halo 2 and Halo 3 (Halo 4 Hunters are probably the hardest)
-Drones can fly all around but they are easier to dispatch with rifles and sub-machine guns
-Brutes have armor but can lose it with repetitive shots and/or energy weapons and be more vulnerable to head shots
-Flood forms are mostly close-combat and can have weapons and shields, but most are vulnerable to head shots and grenades, plus the infection forms are more dangerous in numbers. Be aware that in Halo 3 they can change shape, from long-range foes to fast foes to slow-and-methodical foes, so keep both eyes and ears out.
-Sentinel enemies are fast and teleport like crazy, especially the Knights; those Knights are very tough.
-Engineers in Halo 3: ODST and Halo: Reach are enemies that strengthen enemy shields in combat; they are vulnerable to plasma weapons and must be destroyed to make battles more easier.
—Allies for the most part help you out most of the time, but sometimes they throw grenades and miss and end up killing themselves, and in Halo 3 they are NOTORIOUS for launching rockets on mongeese and hitting their allies; maybe the most unreliable allies in any Halo game ever. The Arbiter is is good; in Halo 3 he distracts enemies and temporarily dies, then once the enemies are cleared he magically comes back.

[h1][b][u]Story[/u][/b][/h1]
Halo: Reach—There is only one word that perfectly describes the entirety of the story for this game: sacrifice. This story has meaning.
Halo: CE—Kill Covenant, land on Halo, rescue the Captain, figure out what Halo is, discover something awful, get involved in a crossfire, fly to the Autumn, blow something up, and escape. We're just getting started.
Halo 2—Betrayal, religious conspiracy, distrust, separation, and as an insult(?) possibly the worst cliffhanger ever.
Halo 3—Kill Brutes, ride vehicles, blow sh*t up, post-traumatic Spartan disorder, sacrifice, and keeping a promise.
Halo 3: ODST—Survival, teamwork, and freedom.
Halo 4—Vulnerability, degradation, and compassion. In short, it made me cry.

[h1][b][u]Bosses[/u][/b][/h1]
Not really a lot of boss fights. None in Halo: CE and Halo 3: ODST. Halo: Reach has a small boss fight, Halo 2 has two fights, Halo 3 has a scripted boss fight near the end, and Halo 4 has a heavily-scripted boss fight. Otherwise, LOTS and LOTS of enemies to kill.

[h1][b][u]Graphics[/u][/b][/h1]
Graphics can be switched on the fly in Halo: CE and Halo 2 from the old graphics to the new graphics with a touch of a button. There are three graphical presets: Original, Enhanced, and Performance presets. There are probably more options that will release for later games, but those are the default I've heard most about.

[h1][b][u]Music[/u][/b][/h1]
Martin O'Donnell and Michael Salvatori wrote some of the best music that I've ever heard since the release of the first game, and to this day it still manages to bring me back. 343, Pyramind Studios , and Sumthing Else Music also did a fantastic job with the remastered editions as well. I prefer the former soundtrack and highly recommend that you listen to it.

If you have not played Halo before, than expect 6 full length (~8 hours/game) campaigns that are very enjoyable alongside multiplayer that fans have loved for years.

Side Note: [b]Microsoft please release Halo Infinite on Steam[b]

- Gameplay : 

When everything is working perfectly it's easy to see why this franchise was seen as being so revolutionary in it's day. Between the dramatic pacing of these stories and the memorial battles that take place, it's easy to understand why more titles in this genre made an effort to be more like Halo. Halo 2 and Halo 3 stand out spectacularly in this department while Halo: CEA is still a classic albeit, noticeably aged experience, and Halo 4 feels nearly out of place as the first in 343 Industries brand of Halo games. A universal control scheme ties it all together in a seamless fashion and the 60 frames per-second really helps things. When all kinds of human and covenant weapons start firing in multiple directions you can really tell the difference and I don't imagine I'll want to play an FPS at a lower frame-rate ever again. It's that profound.



- Graphics : 

The original graphics are the best they have ever looked, Thats to say, they range from dated, to ugly, but it's still easy to see how they were considered AAA for there time. Most of the problems have to do with the actual art-style inconsistency between the games. The original graphics of Halo 2 and Halo 3 could be two parts to the same game, bombing around in war-torn cities and far-off worlds is where Halo is at home, and it's never more apparent than in those games. On the flip-side, Halo 4 has a a very clean, straightforward, and "new" feel to it while Halo: CEA retains its more lived-in atmosphere with the alien-world feel to it all. In order to save time with Halo 2, 343i borrowed several art assets from Halo 4, and it leads to a few instances of losing your sense of time passed within the lore. Seeing the Halo 4 warthog model in Halo 2 Anniversary really takes you out of the experience and is a small but dramatic oversight. Technically, nothing is pushing the Xbox One in any real way here but I can't imagine these games looking any better than they already do.

The following is less of a review of the game, more of a throwback to some different times.

Originally a very experimental game by Bungie turned into Microsofts biggest selling IPs and probably one major contributor to the console Xbox's growth. Originally as a fan of Halo CE on PC I have journeyed through the roller coaster that was Microsoft and their orientation picking process, like following the needle of a broken compass.

To me, it's very fascinating that Microsoft for so many years tried to distantiate themselves from the PC gaming scene. Despite them being the developers of the Windows operating system and ergo the majority of potential customers right in front of them. Yes, yes, PC gaming was having some tough times and Microsoft certainly did not help. "Halo 2 for Windows Vista" they called it, which not only had the repulsive "Games for Windows Live" DRM, but some sort of pseudo console adaptation where the game was solely limited to glorious Windows Vista.

It went dark, no more adventure of Master Chief and Cortana on the Windows PC. Microsoft was all set to make Halo the cornerstone of Xbox sales. Halo 3, Halo 3: ODST, Halo Reach, Halo 4 and Halo 5 were all Xbox exclusives, with the latter two being developed by 343 Industries rather than Bungie who instead left their partnership with Microsoft.

Halo: The Master Chief Collection was originally a remaster specifically for Xbox One and was a major selling point for the console and the reason why I got Xbox One. It originally only consisted of the first 3 Halo games, as those are indeed the character Master Chief's saga. Over the years though ODST, Reach and Halo 4 got ported over too, and the game was released on, not only PC but on Steam as well. Halo 5 remains Xbox One exclusive, but Halo Infinite - the upcoming title in the series is set to release on both platforms.

Even though Microsoft has acknowledged that the PC gaming scene exists, "Video Games" and "Xbox" must be synonyms to them, as everything regarding games are labeled as "Xbox", even on PC.

Anyway, MCC is great. Countless of hours in both single player and multiplayer and a very reasonable price tag. The developers amazingly lived up to their word and released all six games within a year.

Preface: I am a big halo fan. The Halo Bungie games will always be very special to me, and I will probably revisit these games throughout my entire life. I will try and be as unbiased as I can be, and this review will likely change time goes on, and as the other games are released, but here are my thoughts. 


[h1]For Players who know Halo:[/h1]

The first release of MCC(For xbox one in 2014) was one of the biggest disappointments I've had when it comes to gaming. I was hoping it would bring a resurgence for halo, but it ended up feeling like, at least for me, some of the final nails in the coffin. I lost all faith in 343 Industries after this, and halo 5 only confirmed my feelings (despite being an objectively better game than halo 4 in all aspects but story), which caused me to fully transitioned to PC gaming. 

Skip ahead to now, with a PC release for the MCC, and what seems like a fresh start for 343, one where they listen to the community and do their best to remedy their mistakes. 

[b]The launch of Reach has been great so far[/b], with things working seamlessly. Me and my friends have nothing but good things to say so far. 
Strong dedicated servers, good controls, the FOV slider works great, and the uncapped framerate has given me zero issues so far. I would say this is an example of a great port, and any significant blemishes have yet to show. 


[h1]For players new to halo:[/h1]
There is a reason halo is a household name for gaming. Despite its simplistic style, the game has a huge amount of depth, with lots to offer for both casual and competitive players. 
For Reach specifically:
The campaign is one of the best in the series, and I would highly recommend it to anyone, with the capability of CO-OP up to 4 people, there is a ton of fun to be had. The campaign was designed with a lot of attention to detail, with a lot of easter eggs and things to accomplish, and an engaging story. 
For casual multiplayer and custom games, reach has a lot to offer. From racing, zombies, and jump puzzles, to capture the flag, KOTH, and VIP. There are a ton of modes, and now that it is on PC, the sky is the limit for what you can do and make. There is also a firefight mode, which is essentially a survival gametype, that you can solo or coop with others. 
Now for competitive multiplayer, Reach is not my favorite halo title. It is the title that introduced non-arena aspects to the series. However it still retains the identity of halo, and is an [b]excellent FPS[/b], which is still completely skill-focused.

Ever since i started playing video games I've been hearing about Halo and what an amazing franchise it is, after finally playing through the games in this collection i can say they were right. These are some of the best first person shooters I've ever played. From great level design, engaging combat and a phenomenal soundtrack to a great story with deep lore, Halo has it all.

The original trilogy is honestly a perfect story, in Halo 1 you are thrown into this mysterious world and gradually understand what is happening. The second game starts with another side to the story as you learn more about the covenant, while also continuing where Halo 1 left of. 2's campaign is just brilliant and provides us with two different perspectives while expanding upon the story and finally in Halo 3 everything comes to a satisfying conclusion. Halo3:ODST is also set between 2 and 3 and while i think it's the weakest game in the collection it is still interesting and bridges the gap between 2 and 3. Then there is Halo Reach, a prequel to Halo 1 and god it is fantastic. If you play the trilogy first you know what's gonna happen here but that doesn't make any less impactful and as the get closer to the end everything unfolds. It's the last game made by Bungie and they delivered a great sendoff. Lastly there is Halo 4 which i actually liked quite a lot. It tells a stand alone tale and wraps it up in a satisfying way but the standout here is the relationship between Cortana and Chief which was never touched this deeply. These two are so good it makes the whole game worthwhile. 

There is also a ton of replayability with different playlists, collectibles and lore terminals (which are essential for understanding the deeper lore), skulls and the multiplayer which is still active. Honestly 6 good games for the price of one is worth it and if you are interested in a fun shooter with great story and tons of content it is a must play for you.
